name: Jaimini
dates_notes: Jaimini is named in the Brahma-Sūtra as a Vedāntic ācārya and in the Mīmāṃsā-Sūtra as its compiler-author; the relative position of the two sūtra-corpora and their cross-references makes the dating mutually constraining. Frauwallner, Geschichte der indischen Philosophie, places Jaimini in the third to second century BCE. The biographical figure is a name attached to the founding sūtra-text.

lineage_polemical.note: The Brahma-Sūtra's first substantive sūtra after the maṅgala — 1.1.4, tat tu samanvayāt — is read by every later Vedāntic bhāṣyakāra as Bādarāyaṇa's response to the Mīmāṃsā prioritization of the karma-kāṇḍa: śruti's tātparya converges on brahman, not merely on enjoined ritual action. The Brahma-Sūtra cites Jaimini by name on several disputed adhikaraṇas (e.g., 1.2.31, 3.4.2, 4.4.5), the relation is constructive on śruti's pramāṇa-status and polemical on the supremacy of dharma-jijñāsā versus brahma-jijñāsā.

core_thesis: Jaimini is the traditional author of the *Mīmāṃsā-Sūtra*, the foundational text of Pūrva-Mīmāṃsā. It defines *dharma* through Vedic injunction and treats the Veda as an autonomous authority for matters not available to perception or inference. The sūtras provide tools for interpreting injunction, praise, mantra, and naming passages, and for resolving apparent conflicts within ritual texts. They establish central themes developed by later Mīmāṃsakas: the non-human origin and permanence of the Veda, the authority of verbal testimony, and the relation between ritual action and its result. The text provides the framework within which later authors explain *apūrva*, the unseen connection between rite and result, and debate the validity of cognition. Śabara, Kumārila, Prabhākara, and later Mīmāṃsakas develop its compressed arguments in divergent directions.

engaged_works.title: Mimamsa-Sutra
engaged_works.composition_dates_notes: Composition fixed by mutual citation with the Brahma-Sūtra and by the relative position to the early Dharma-Sūtras.
engaged_works.ascription_notes: Uniformly ascribed to Jaimini by tradition; the surviving twelve-adhyāya text is likely the consolidation of an earlier oral sūtra-tradition, paralleling the Brahma-Sūtra's compositional history.

ascription_evidence.description: Frauwallner Geschichte der indischen Philosophie I and Clooney 1990 Thinking Ritually are the standard scholarly references for the ascription; neither work is on disk in our corpus, cited via field-standard summary.

engaged_works.summary: Twelve *adhyāyas*, each in four *pādas*, of about 2745 *sūtras* — the largest of the *darśanika* sūtra-corpora. Clooney's *Thinking Ritually* (1990) is the standard English-language secondary reading of the work as a coherent ritual-cum-reflective system. The first *adhyāya* establishes the foundational doctrines: *codanā* as the autonomous *pramāṇa* for *dharma*, the eternity of *śabda*, the four sentence-types (*vidhi*, *arthavāda*, *mantra*, *nāmadheya*), and the *svataḥ-prāmāṇya* of cognition. *Adhyāyas* 2–6 develop the analytical apparatus for ritual interpretation — the *sad-vidha-tātparya-liṅga* (the six marks of intended meaning), the *aṅga-aṅgi-vibhāga* (analysis of subordinate and principal ritual elements), and the procedure-rules (*prakaraṇa*, *sthāna*, *krama*, *samākhyā*). *Adhyāyas* 7–9 treat *atideśa* — the extension of one ritual's procedure to another — and *bādha*. *Adhyāya* 10 treats *ūha* (modification) and *bādha* (cancellation). *Adhyāya* 11 treats *tantra* (the unification of multiple ritual elements). *Adhyāya* 12 treats *prasaṅga* (the contingent extension of one ritual element to another). The work cites by name the ācāryas Bādari, Bādarāyaṇa, Lābukāyana, and others — direct evidence of an earlier oral *sūtra*-tradition. The text is unintelligible without commentary; the principal commentary is Śabara's *Śābara-Bhāṣya*.
